column5: Pharaoh orders sons cast into the Nile
column6: Pharaoh commands that every Hebrew son be thrown into the Nile. This supplies the lethal political setting that makes Moses' mother's water placement in the commentary a protective counter-use of the same water.

column5: mother bears, sees, and hides Moses
column6: Moses' mother gives birth, sees that he is good, and hides him for three months. This verse supplies the maternal fear and prior home-care that precede the basket scene and the commentary's nursing mother.

column5: tender children and nursing flocks require a slow pace
column6: Jacob refuses to drive on too hard because the children are tender and the flocks and herds are nursing. The verse unusually joins vulnerable children, lactating animals, and measured care, meeting the commentary's child and milk-sheep imagery.

column5: blessings of breasts and womb
column6: Jacob's blessing names the breasts and womb among God's life-giving blessings. It is a concentrated biblical counterpart to the commentary's paired attention to womb, birth, and milk-giving nurture.

column5: Joseph provides for kin and their little ones
column6: Joseph promises to provide for his brothers and their little ones, then comforts them. It makes familial mercy material through food and reassurance, closely fitting the commentary's provisions-in-the-house and mercy-as-beneficence claims.

column5: Israel as God's firstborn son
column6: God calls Israel his firstborn son in the message to Pharaoh. This makes divine lordship a parental relation and gives political force to the commentary's account of the Rabb who nurtures children.

column5: God feeds and clothes the vulnerable outsider
column6: God executes justice for orphan and widow and loves the resident alien by giving food and clothing. It offers a concrete biblical form of the commentary's mercy that bends toward the weak and becomes provision.

column5: God guards Israel as the apple of his eye
column6: The wilderness song says that God found, encircled, cared for, and guarded Israel as the apple of his eye. This is a close biblical companion to Musa being brought up under God's eye rather than merely under Pharaoh's claim.

column5: a parent bird trains and carries its young
column6: The eagle stirs its nest, hovers over its young, spreads wings, takes them, and bears them. Its patient sequence of urging, sheltering, and carrying gives a vivid animal analogue to terbiye as growth through successive states.

column5: God as father who disciplines a son
column6: God promises of David's heir, "I will be his father and he will be my son," and speaks of correction when he errs. This is a direct biblical parent-child account of lordly formation that includes discipline as well as care.

column5: lamb grows inside the household as a daughter
column6: Nathan's poor man's lamb grows up with him and his children, shares food and drink, lies in his bosom, and is like a daughter. It makes the commentary's domestic sheep image into a striking household scene of nurtured dependence.

column5: child and nurse hidden from royal violence
column6: Jehosheba takes the infant Joash with his nurse and hides them in a bedroom from those killing royal children. This is a separate biblical child-preservation scene joining danger, a nurse, concealment, and a substitute household.

column5: God receives the one abandoned by parents
column6: Even if father and mother forsake the speaker, YHWH receives him. It provides a compact divine-foster-parent image beside the commentary's insistence that the one who truly raises a child may be other than the visible household.

column5: quieted soul like a weaned child with its mother
column6: The psalm compares its quieted soul to a weaned child with its mother. It adds the post-nursing stage of peaceful attachment to the commentary's womb, breast, and gradual completion sequence.

column5: train a child in the way to go
column6: The proverb explicitly speaks of training a child for his way so that age will not make him depart from it. It is a concise Hebrew Bible formulation of the commentary's terbiye as directed, enduring formation.

column5: God's work hidden in a pregnant womb
column6: Qoheleth compares the unknowable work of God with not knowing how bones develop in a pregnant woman's womb. The comparison makes prenatal formation an arena of divine hiddenness, complementing the commentary's more affirmative image of God shaping there.

column5: God brings to birth and does not shut the womb
column6: God asks whether the one who brings to birth would fail to cause delivery or shut the womb. It gives a prophetic divine-birth image that directly accompanies the commentary's womb as a place governed by God.

column5: an abandoned newborn lacks ordinary care
column6: Jerusalem is figured as a newborn whose cord is not cut and who is not washed, salted, or swaddled. This negative picture makes bodily care of a weak infant the test case for the mercy and household nurture developed in the commentary.

column5: God sees the exposed infant and commands life
column6: God passes the infant abandoned in blood and says, "Live." The rescue turns compassion toward a helpless child into decisive action, directly illuminating the commentary's definition of mercy as beneficence toward the weak.

column5: rescued infant grows to mature bodily fullness
column6: In the continuing infant allegory, God causes the child to grow and arrive at maturity. The verse supplies a disturbing but precise prophetic instance of growth from exposure toward fullness, making the commentary's state-by-state completion image less sentimental.

column5: two opposed peoples issue from one womb
column6: God tells Rebekah that two nations and divided peoples are in her womb. It qualifies the commentary's association of one womb with kinship by showing a biblical womb that contains rivalry and eventual separation.

column5: compassionate mothers reversed by famine
column6: In siege, women called compassionate cook their own children for food. This horrific reversal makes maternal compassion and household nourishment collapse into their opposites, a counter-image to the commentary's merciful womb-home.

column5: God retains the key of childbirth
column6: The Bavli lists childbirth among the keys that God does not entrust to an intermediary, grounding it in Rachel's opened womb. This is a direct Jewish interpretive assertion of the divine agency behind the commentary's womb and birth images.

column5: parental duties of bodily, Torah, and vocational formation
column6: The Bavli enumerates a father's obligations toward a son, including circumcision, redemption, Torah instruction, marriage, and a trade. It gives a concrete rabbinic map of upbringing that moves beyond birth toward a child's completed social and religious formation.

column5: communal teachers for children
column6: The account of Joshua ben Gamla's school reform makes accessible teachers for children a communal duty. It develops the commentary's teacher-nurturer image into an institutional form of care for learners who cannot yet sustain themselves.

column5: an infant responds within the mother's womb
column6: At Mary's greeting, the infant leaps in Elizabeth's womb and she is filled with the Holy Spirit. The scene gives the womb a responsive sacred interior, alongside the commentary's womb as a divinely active place of formation.

column5: compassion for a bereaved mother and her only son
column6: Jesus sees the bereaved widow and is moved with compassion before addressing her loss. The scene places mercy beside a mother's emptied household and anticipates restoration of her child, close to the commentary's maternal grief and return motif.

column5: womb and breasts praised for bearing and nursing Jesus
column6: A woman blesses the womb that bore Jesus and the breasts he nursed. This is an unusually explicit New Testament meeting with the commentary's womb-as-home and maternal-nourishment language.

column5: blessedness redirected to hearing and keeping God's word
column6: Jesus answers the blessing of womb and breasts by pronouncing blessed those who hear and keep God's word. The response does not erase the preceding maternal image, but redirects its privileged meaning toward received teaching, a contrast central to the commentary's womb-to-learning movement.

column5: the Father's will that no little one perish
column6: Jesus states that the heavenly Father does not will the loss of even one little one. It is a precise divine-parental articulation of mercy toward the weak child.

column5: birth from God rather than blood or human will
column6: The prologue describes those born not from blood, fleshly will, or a man's will, but from God. It offers a Johannine redescription of descent that stands in productive tension with the commentary's bodily womb and kinship account.

column5: Moses instructed in Egyptian wisdom
column6: Stephen says Moses was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and became powerful in words and deeds. It supplies the educational continuation of the foster-household narrative, relevant to the commentary's move from being raised to being taught.

column5: adoption and the cry Abba, Father
column6: The Spirit of adoption enables believers to cry, "Abba, Father." This makes nonbiological incorporation into a parental divine household an explicit Christian counterpart to the commentary's birth-parent and foster-parent distinctions.

column5: spiritual fatherhood exceeds guardianship
column6: Paul contrasts many guardians in Christ with his singular fatherhood through the gospel. It gives a particularly close Christian distinction between a supervising caregiver and a formative parent, matching the commentary's careful nonbirth-parent vocabulary.

column5: leaving childhood ways for adulthood
column6: Paul uses the passage from child to adult as the figure for a completed mode of knowing. It is a brief but exact New Testament staging of maturation that belongs beside terbiye's movement toward completion.

column5: parents store up for children
column6: Paul invokes the household norm that parents should save for children, not children for parents. It directly connects parenthood with provision, complementing the commentary's domestic food and child-rearing images.

column5: God's son born of a woman
column6: God sends his Son, born of a woman and under the law. The verse keeps incarnation within a concrete maternal birth while the surrounding argument moves toward adoption, furnishing both sides of the commentary's womb and foster-family frame.

column5: nourishing and cherishing as embodied care
column6: A person nourishes and cherishes his own body, as Christ does the church. The verb for nourishing extends the commentary's rearing imagery into a Christian account of sustained, intimate care.

column5: children repay parents through care for their household
column6: Children and grandchildren must first practice piety toward their own household and make return to their parents. This is a direct New Testament counterpart to the commentary's Qur'an 17:23–24 reversal from parental raising to a child's merciful responsibility.

column5: Sacred writings known from infancy
column6: Timothy has known the sacred writings from infancy, which can make him wise for salvation. It is a direct image of instruction beginning in childhood and reaching mature discernment.

column5: milk and elementary instruction before mature teaching
column6: The readers, who should be teachers, need the elementary words again and have become people needing milk. It adds the pedagogical problem behind the commentary's image of feeding learners small pieces of knowledge.

column5: fatherly discipline addressed to a son
column6: The exhortation cites the address, "My son," and tells the child not to reject the Lord's discipline. This supplies the explicit father-son language whose later training result appears in Heb. 12:11.

column5: straight paths heal what is weak
column6: After the discipline argument, hearers are told to make straight paths for their feet so that what is lame may be healed. It links the commentary's straight path to formative care for the weak rather than to direction alone.

column5: compassion fails without food and clothing
column6: James rejects telling an inadequately clothed and hungry sibling to depart in peace without giving what the body needs. It makes the commentary's mercy-to-beneficence claim a sharply practical test involving household necessities.

column5: Mary's childhood nourishment in the temple
column6: In the common chapter division, three-year-old Mary is placed at the temple and receives food from an angel. This infancy tradition adds a distinctly Christian scene of a child reared outside her parents' home; chapter and verse divisions vary by translation.

column5: God creates humans to grow toward perfection
column6: Irenaeus argues that created humanity must grow gradually toward perfection rather than receive its final capacity all at once. This patristic account gives a theological analogue to the commentary's definition of terbiye as movement through states to completion.
